clue.text: Hungry strict religious group given food outside

indicators.note: outside says the letters for being given food sit around the religious group

parts.note: to be given food is to be fed
the Amish are a strict Anabaptist sect in the USA

explanation.surface: A hungry member of a strict sect is offered a meal from outside the community.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone starving or ravenous is extremely hungry; the word is a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Heartless Scandinavian murder?

indicators.note: heartless means the central letter of the word is cut out

parts.note: someone from Finland is Finnish, loosely counted as Scandinavian

explanation.surface: A Nordic crime novel: a cold-blooded Scandinavian killing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heartless' removes the middle N of the seven-letter word. The question mark flags that the definition is an informal sense: to finish someone off is to kill them.
explanation.definitionFit: To finish off a victim is slang for killing them, so the verb can stand for murder.

clue.text: Field of research that could produce essential ceramic

indicators.note: could produce says these letters can be rearranged to produce something else

explanation.surface: Describes an academic discipline that might develop some vital new ceramic.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is almost literal, since this discipline does study ceramics; 'could produce' is the anagram signal working on all sixteen letters of 'essential ceramic'.
explanation.definitionFit: Materials science is an academic discipline studying the properties of substances such as metals, polymers and ceramics.

clue.text: See 2
Character revealed by stethoscope

indicators.note: revealed by says the letters are found lying inside the next word

explanation.surface: A doctor's listening instrument exposes a patient's true nature.
explanation.definitionFit: An ethos is the characteristic spirit or nature of a person or community.

clue.text: Like this clue? Annoyed with answer given first

indicators.note: given first puts the letter for answer ahead of the word for annoyed

parts.note: someone annoyed is cross

explanation.surface: A self-referential teaser that pretends to be a grumpy puzzler talking about the clue in front of them.
explanation.definitionFit: This clue sits in the horizontal list of the grid, so it is literally one of the across clues.

clue.text: Mythical creature of unusual nature with colt's head

indicators.note: the head of the word for a young horse is its first letter
unusual tells us the letters of the next word appear in an unusual order

explanation.surface: A legendary beast of strange character that has the head of a young horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head' takes C from 'colt's', and 'unusual' rearranges NATURE into ENTAUR. The surface misleads: the creature actually has a horse's body and a man's head.
explanation.definitionFit: A centaur is a figure from Greek legend, half man and half horse.

clue.text: Leaves American university so upset about it

indicators.note: about it means the turned word wraps around the university just named
upset in a down clue means the little word is turned over, read from bottom to top

parts.note: MIT is the Massachusetts Institute of Technology

explanation.surface: Someone departs from an American college, so troubled by the matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns the little word over into OS; 'about it' wraps that round the Massachusetts college just named.
explanation.definitionFit: To leave out something is to omit it, so leaves in that sense works as a synonym.

clue.text: After slump a financial centre shows good sense

indicators.note: after says the following pieces come behind the word for slump

parts.note: to slump is to sag
the City is London's financial district

explanation.surface: Following a market crash, a financial district behaves prudently.
explanation.walkthrough: THE CITY is the City of London, the financial district.
explanation.definitionFit: Sagacity is wisdom and sound judgement, a near synonym for good sense.

clue.text: Break code — task providing defence

indicators.note: to break something is to smash it apart, so the letters of the two words are broken up and reformed

explanation.surface: Cracking a secret cipher is a mission that protects the nation.
explanation.definitionFit: A stockade is a barrier of upright stakes built as a defensive enclosure.

clue.text: Yet this is how all-seater stadiums are

definitions.meaning: a conjunction meaning however or nevertheless

definitions.text: this is how all-seater stadiums are
definitions.meaning: read as three words, a stadium where everyone sits is ... room

explanation.surface: Seems to be a remark about modern football grounds with seats for every spectator.
explanation.walkthrough: All-seater stadiums became compulsory in top English football after 1989; the second sense splits the answer into NOT WITH STANDING.
explanation.definitionFit: Notwithstanding can mean nevertheless or all the same, the sense of yet as a sentence adverb.

clue.text: Trick cyclists needing quiet places to skate

parts.note: SH is a call for quiet
ice skaters go round rinks

explanation.surface: Circus stunt riders want some peaceful arenas to roller-skate in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trick cyclists' is old British rhyming-ish slang for psychiatrists, from 'psychiatrist' sounding like 'cyclist'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrink is slang for a psychiatrist, and so is trick cyclist, so the plurals match.

clue.text: Get along fine mostly putting donkey in prestigious event

indicators.note: in places the animal inside the shortened word
mostly means the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: people who get along fine click
an ass is a donkey

explanation.surface: Racing talk: things go well when a donkey is entered in a top race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' leaves CLIC, and 'putting ... in' places the animal inside. The Classics are Britain's five top flat horse races, such as the Derby.
explanation.definitionFit: A classic is a major, long-established sporting contest, notably one of the big flat races.

clue.text: Mediterranean city's greeting to departing North American spies

parts.note: vale is Latin for farewell, said to someone leaving
the CIA is the US intelligence agency

explanation.surface: A Spanish port bids farewell to American secret agents leaving the country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'North American' looks like one phrase but splits: N for North, CIA for the American spies.
explanation.definitionFit: Valencia is a Spanish port city on the Mediterranean coast.

clue.text: Tribal leader making a lot of noise

parts.note: a clan is a tribal group, so clan works as the attributive
a king is a leader

explanation.surface: A chief of a tribe is being loud.
explanation.definitionFit: Clanking is a loud metallic rattling, so something clanking is noisy.

clue.text: Just offside?

definitions.meaning: the offside of a British car is the side nearest the middle of the road, the driver's side

explanation.surface: Sounds like a football fan asking whether a player was only marginally offside.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain, cars drive on the left, so a vehicle's offside is its right-hand side; football's offside rule is the red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: Right means just or morally correct, and right is the offside of a British vehicle.

clue.text: Stop fool flying — it's not worth much apparently

parts.note: to stop a pilot from flying is to ground them; 'flying' completes this sense
a nut is a crazy person, a fool

explanation.surface: An order to keep a madman out of the air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stop ... flying' together means GROUND. The definition plays on 'peanuts', meaning a trivial sum.
explanation.definitionFit: A groundnut is a peanut, and peanuts is slang for a paltry amount of money.

clue.text: Two jazz fans going head to head, coming in so jumpily?

indicators.note: coming in means the pair goes inside the little word
two creatures meeting head to head face each other, so the first is turned to face the second

parts.note: cats are jazz fans in old slang; two of them give CAT twice

explanation.surface: Two jazz lovers clash and enter so nervously.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two jazz fans' gives two cats; 'going head to head' turns the first round so the heads meet, making TACCAT, which 'coming in' puts inside the little word 'so'.
explanation.definitionFit: Staccato is a musical direction for short, detached notes, so played jerkily or jumpily.

clue.text: Hardy heroine takes in tense international matches

indicators.note: takes in means the heroine's name holds the next letter inside

parts.note: Tess of the d'Urbervilles is Thomas Hardy's heroine
T is the grammar abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: A literary heroine sits through some edgy international fixtures.
explanation.walkthrough: Test matches are full international cricket or rugby games.
explanation.definitionFit: Tests are the top-level international fixtures in cricket and rugby.

clue.text: Swimmer's aid — something to help one see coming up round Orkney — not half

indicators.note: round means the upturned letters go around the island fragment
coming up in a down clue means read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a lens helps one see

indicators.note: not half keeps only half of the island's name, its first half

explanation.surface: A diver's gear, plus a device to see Orkney as it looms into view, only partly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming up' gives SNEL, 'not half' keeps the island's first three letters, and 'round' puts the turned word around them.
explanation.definitionFit: A snorkel is a breathing tube that lets a swimmer stay face down in the water.

clue.text: Dislike state's entity having charge

parts.note: state's read as 'states' gives avers, as in to state firmly
an ion is a particle carrying an electric charge

explanation.surface: Political-sounding: a country resents some body being put in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'state's' is read as the verb 'states', so it gives AVERS.
explanation.definitionFit: An aversion is a strong dislike or antipathy.

clue.text: Fail to pay attention that's small inconvenience

parts.note: to lumber someone is to burden them, so lumber is an inconvenience

explanation.surface: Not listening is only a minor nuisance.
explanation.definitionFit: To slumber is to sleep or doze, so it is a way of not paying attention.

clue.text: Fashion shops stocking unknown fragrant plant

indicators.note: stocking means holding inside, as a shop stocks goods
to fashion is to shape, so the letters of shops are reshaped

parts.note: Y is an algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: Boutiques selling a little-known perfumed herb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fashion' rearranges SHOPS into HSSOP, and 'stocking' puts Y inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Hyssop is an aromatic herb of the mint family.

clue.text: What clergy wear suit mostly needing belt?

indicators.note: mostly means the final letter of the lawsuit word is dropped

parts.note: a lawsuit is a case
to belt or sock someone is to hit them

explanation.surface: A wry question about vestments: a long garment that mostly needs a girdle?
explanation.walkthrough: 'belt' looks like clothing in this surface but means a punch.
explanation.definitionFit: A cassock is the full-length robe worn by priests and choristers.

clue.text: Dressing for dance

definitions.meaning: a spicy sauce or relish served over food

explanation.surface: Putting on clothes ready for a night out dancing.
explanation.definitionFit: Salsa is a spicy tomato sauce and also a Latin dance style.

clue.text: Competition needing horses you rent out

indicators.note: out means the letters are put out of order

explanation.surface: A contest with mounts that you hire out to riders.
explanation.definitionFit: A tourney is a medieval tournament in which knights jousted on horseback.

clue.text: Dance beat requiring energy

parts.note: to tan someone's hide is to beat them
go means energy or vigour

explanation.surface: A dance rhythm that needs lots of vigour.
explanation.definitionFit: The tango is a ballroom dance originating in Argentina.

clue.text: Emaciated condition in lank lads treated by doctor

indicators.note: treated means worked on, so the letters are reprocessed into a new order

parts.note: Bones is the nickname of Dr McCoy in Star Trek, and slang for a doctor

explanation.surface: A doctor attends to thin youngsters suffering from malnutrition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'treated' rearranges IN plus LANKLADS into ALLSKINAND; 'doctor' is BONES, a slang name for a medic, not an anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone all skin and bones is so thin their skeleton shows, the state of being emaciated.

clue.text: Speaking role finally censored from 'Love Actually'

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, the letter O

indicators.note: censored from means the letter is cut out of the following word

parts.note: actually can mean really

indicators.note: finally picks out the final letter of the word before

explanation.surface: An actor's speaking part was cut from the romantic comedy film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love Actually' looks like the 2003 film title but splits into O and REALLY; 'role finally' gives E, which 'censored from' cuts.
explanation.definitionFit: Orally means by speaking, by word of mouth.

clue.text: Block group from circa 1970 reaching number one

parts.note: the Doors were Jim Morrison's rock band of the late 1960s
top means first, number one

explanation.surface: A rock band of around 1970 is kept from reaching the top of the charts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Block' reads as a verb about stopping the band, but it is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A doorstop is a wedge or heavy block used to hold a door open.
